Milwaukee is the most populous city in Wisconsin.
The county seat of Milwaukee County is Milwaukee.
At the 2020 census, Milwaukee's population was 577,222.
Milwaukee is the 31st-most populous city in the United States.
Milwaukee is the fifth-most populous city in the Midwest.
Milwaukee is the central city of the Milwaukee metropolitan area.
The Milwaukee metropolitan area has a population of 1.57 million residents.
Milwaukee is an ethnically and culturally diverse city.
Milwaukee continues to be one of the most racially segregated cities, largely due to early-20th-century redlining.
German immigrants heavily influenced Milwaukee's history in the 19th century.
The Milwaukee metropolitan area has a regional GDP of over $102 billion in 2020.
Summerfest is held annually in Milwaukee since 1968.
Milwaukee hosts various cultural events, including German Fest and Oktoberfest.
The name "Milwaukee" is disputed; some theories suggest it comes from the Anishinaabemowin/Ojibwe word meaning "good land."
The city of Milwaukee claims that the name is derived from mahn-ah-wauk, a Potawatomi word for "council grounds."
The name "Milwaukee" was spelled in many ways prior to 1844.
The Milwaukee Sentinel used Milwaukie in its headline until it switched to Milwaukee on November 30, 1844.
Indigenous cultures lived along the waterways for thousands of years before European contact.

The first recorded inhabitants of the Milwaukee area were various Native American tribes: Menominee, Fox, Mascouten, Sauk, Potawatomi, and Ojibwe (Algic/Algonquian peoples), and Ho-Chunk (Winnebago, a Siouan people).
During the French and Indian War, a group of "Ojibwas and Pottawattamies" joined the French-Canadian Daniel Liénard de Beaujeu at the Battle of the Monongahela.
The Native Americans around Milwaukee were some of the few groups to ally with the rebel Continentals during the American Revolutionary War.
After the American Revolutionary War, the Native Americans fought the United States in the Northwest Indian War as part of the Council of Three Fires.
During the War of 1812, a council was held in Milwaukee in June 1812, which resulted in their decision to attack Chicago in retaliation against American expansion.
The Battle of Fort Dearborn on August 15, 1812, is the only known armed conflict in Chicago.
The American government removed these groups of Native Americans from their indigenous land after being attacked in the Black Hawk War in 1832.
Solomon Juneau was the first to come to the area in 1818 and founded a town called Juneautown.
Byron Kilbourn established Kilbourntown west of the Milwaukee River, competing with Juneautown.
George H. Walker claimed land south of the Milwaukee River, building a log house there in 1834.
The first large wave of settlement to areas that would later become Milwaukee County and the City of Milwaukee began in 1835 following the removal of tribes in the Council of Three Fires.
By September 17, 1835, the first election was held in Milwaukee with 39 votes cast.
On January 31, 1846, the towns were combined to incorporate as the City of Milwaukee and elected Solomon Juneau as its first mayor.
The German presence in Milwaukee after the Civil War remained strong.
Polish immigrants made their way to Milwaukee for low-paying entry-level jobs.
Milwaukee has the fifth-largest Polish population in the U.S. at 45,467.
The largest Italian-American festival in the area is Festa Italiana.
The largest Irish-American festival in southeast Wisconsin is Irishfest.
European descendants ("Whites") represented 99.7% of Milwaukee's total population of 373,857 in 1910.
Milwaukee has a strong Greek Orthodox community with many attending the Annunciation Greek Orthodox Church on Milwaukee's northwest side.
The American Serb Hall is known for its Friday fish fries and popular events.
Many U.S. presidents have visited Milwaukee's Serb Hall in the past.
The Bosnian population is growing in Milwaukee due to late-20th-century immigration after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
A small community of African Americans migrated from the South during the Great Migration.
Bronzeville became a known community for African Americans who settled near each other.
Industry boomed, attracting more migrants and increasing African-American influence in Milwaukee.
By 1925, around 9,000 Mexicans lived in Milwaukee but many moved back south due to the Great Depression.
In the 1950s, the Hispanic community was beginning to emerge as they arrived for jobs in manufacturing and agriculture.
During this time, labor shortages were due to reduced immigration from Eastern and Southern Europe.
Strikes also contributed to labor shortages during this period.
A small community of African Americans migrated from Chicago to Milwaukee's North side in the late 1960s.
The East Side has attracted a population of Russians and other Eastern Europeans since the end of the Cold War.
By 1960, Milwaukee had grown to become one of the largest cities in the United States with a population peak at 741,324.
In 1960, the city was still among the most segregated of that time.
The population of Milwaukee by 2010 was 594,833.
Milwaukee's European history is evident today as it was named one of the "Dozen Distinctive Destinations" by the National Trust for Historic Preservation in 2006.
Historic Milwaukee walking tours provide a guided tour of Milwaukee's historic districts.
The city has a total area of 96.80 square miles, with 96.12 square miles being land and 0.68 square miles being water.
The terrain includes steep bluffs along Lake Michigan that begin about a mile north of downtown.
Milwaukee is located at the confluence of three rivers: Menomonee, Kinnickinnic, and Milwaukee.
Smaller rivers such as Root River and Lincoln Creek also flow through the city.
The tallest building in the city is the U.S. Bank Center, completed in 1973.
Milwaukee's climate is humid continental with cold snowy winters and hot humid summers.
The warmest month of the year is July, with a mean temperature of 73.3°F (22.9°C).
January is the coldest month, with a mean temperature of 24.0°F (-4.4°C).
Milwaukee's location near Lake Michigan influences its climate through lake breezes.
The lake moderates cold air outbreaks during winter months.
Overnight lows in downtown Milwaukee are often warmer than suburban locations due to the urban heat island effect.
Thunderstorms can be dangerous and damaging, bringing hail and high winds.
Almost all summer rainfall is brought by these storms.
Milwaukee's population has dropped at every census count since 1970.
In 2012, Milwaukee was listed as a gamma city by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network.
The population density in 2020 was 6,001.2 inhabitants per square mile (2,317.1/km²).
There were 257,723 housing units at an average density of 2,679.5 per square mile (1,034.6/km²) in 2020.
The population was 20.1% Hispanic or Latino of any race in 2020.

When grouping both Hispanic and non-Hispanic people together by race, the city was 38.6% Black or African American, 36.1% White, 5.2% Asian, 0.9% Native American, 9.0% from other races, and 10.1% from two or more races.
The median income for a household in the city was $43,125 in 2020.
The median income for a family was $51,170 in 2020.
Male full-time workers had a median income of $42,859 versus $37,890 for female workers.
The per capita income for the city was $24,167 in 2020.
About 19.6% of families and 24.6% of the population were below the poverty line in 2020.
In 2015, Milwaukee was rated as the "worst city for black Americans" based on disparities in employment and income levels.
The Milwaukee metropolitan area was cited as being the most segregated in the U.S. in a Jet Magazine article in 2002.
St. Josaphat Basilica is located in Milwaukee's historic Lincoln Village.
As of 2010, approximately 51.8% of residents in the Milwaukee area said they regularly attended religious services.
The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Milwaukee and the Episcopal Diocese of Milwaukee are headquartered in Milwaukee.
The School Sisters of the Third Order of St Francis have their mother house in Milwaukee.

Milwaukee is home to several Lutheran synods, including the Greater Milwaukee Synod of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America; the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod (LCMS), which operates Concordia University Wisconsin in Mequon and Milwaukee Lutheran High School, the nation's oldest Lutheran high school; and the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod (WELS).
The St. Sava Serbian Orthodox Cathedral is a landmark of the Serbian community in Milwaukee.
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has a presence in the Milwaukee area with two stakes among them.
Milwaukee Public Schools (MPS) is the largest school district in Wisconsin and thirty-third in the nation as of 2007.
As of 2006, it employed 11,100 full-time and substitute teachers in 323 schools.
In 2007, 17 MPS high schools appeared on a national list of "dropout factories."
Milwaukee is home to over two dozen private or parochial high schools such as Marquette University High School.
The Milwaukee Public Market is an indoor market that sells produce, seafood, meats, cheeses, vegetables, candies, and flowers from local businesses.
Milwaukee has been a Democratic stronghold for more than a century at the federal level.
At the local level, Socialists often won the mayorship during much of the first sixty years of the 20th century.
The city is split between seven State Senate districts, each divided between three state Assembly districts.

All but four state legislators representing the city are Democrats; the four Republicans represent outer portions of the city that are part of districts dominated by heavily Republican suburban counties.
In 2008, Barack Obama won Milwaukee with 77% of the vote.
The city's population was spread out in 2000, with 28.6% under the age of 18, 12.2% from 18 to 24, 30.2% from 25 to 44, 18.1% from 45 to 64, and 10.9% who were 65 years of age or older.
The median age was 31 years in 2000.
For every 100 females, there were 91.6 males.
For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 87.2 males.
In 2000, the Census estimated at least 1,408 same-sex households in Milwaukee.
Gay-friendly communities have developed primarily in Walker's Point, Bay View, Historic Third Ward, Washington Heights, Riverwest, and the East Side.
In 2001, Milwaukee was named the #1 city for lesbians by Girlfriends magazine.
The Milwaukee Police Department's Gang Unit was reactivated in 2004 after Nannette Hegerty was sworn in as chief.
In 2006, 4,000 charges were brought against suspects through Milwaukee's Gang Unit.
In 2013 there were 105 murders in the city and 87 homicides the following year.
In 2015, 146 people were killed in the city.
In 2018, Milwaukee was ranked the eighth most dangerous city in the US.
As of 2016, Milwaukee currently ranks as the second poorest U.S. city with over 500,000 residents.
In 2013, a Point-In-Time survey estimated 1,500 people were homeless on Milwaukee's streets each night.
The city's homeless and poor are aided by several local nonprofits, including the Milwaukee Rescue Mission.
Milwaukee is home to seven Fortune 500 companies: Johnson Controls, Northwestern Mutual, Fiserv, Manpower, Rockwell Automation, Harley-Davidson, and WEC Energy Group.

Other companies based in Milwaukee include Briggs & Stratton, Brady Corporation, Baird (investment bank), Alliance Federated Energy, Sensient Technologies, Marshall & Ilsley (acquired by BMO Harris Bank in 2010), Hal Leonard, Direct Supply, Rite-Hite, the American Society for Quality, A. O. Smith, Rexnord, Master Lock, Marcus Corporation, REV Group, American Signal Corporation, GE Healthcare, Diagnostic Imaging and Clinical Systems, and MGIC Investments.
The Milwaukee metropolitan area ranks fifth in the United States in terms of the number of Fortune 500 company headquarters as a share of the population.
Milwaukee has a large number of financial service firms, particularly those specializing in mutual funds and transaction processing systems.
A number of publishing and printing companies are also based in Milwaukee.
Service and managerial jobs are the fastest-growing segments of the Milwaukee economy.
Health care alone makes up 27% of the jobs in the city.
Milwaukee is a popular location for sailing, boating, and kayaking on Lake Michigan.
Ethnic dining and cultural festivals take place throughout the summer at Henry Maier Festival Park.
Museums such as the Milwaukee Art Museum and Layton Art Gallery are located in the city.
The Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra performs regularly in the area.
Milwaukee has a long history of musical activity, including the first organized musical society called "Milwaukee Beethoven Society" formed in 1843.
Saengerfeste were held regularly due to large concentrations of German and other European immigrants.
Les Paul and Liberace launched their careers in Milwaukee music venues.
Paramount Records was founded in Grafton, a northern suburb of Milwaukee, in the 1920s and 1930s.
Hal Leonard Corporation is headquartered in Milwaukee.

Milwaukee has over 140 parks with over 15,000 acres of parks and parkways.

The Milwaukee Public Market offers programming for adults and children from its branches located in Riverside Park, Washington Park, and the Menomonee Valley (near Three Bridges Park).
